newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Far East Gold - Confidence shaken after Iraq crisis.
newsitem.headline: Far East Gold - Confidence shaken after Iraq crisis.

text.p: Confidence in gold's usual fourth quarter rally appeared to be eroding this week after the metal's dismal performance during the latest Gulf crisis which saw two U.S. missile attacks on Iraq, dealers said on Friday.
"Oil shot up on the Iraq fighting, but gold only gained 50 cents (an ounce) so afterwards we saw disappointed fund liquidation," one Singapore-based dealer said.

Another dealer said he now believed spot gold would break down through strong support around the US$385 an ounce level and trigger sell-stops sending it towards the $382-$383 area where it might again be able to mount a rally.

Hong Kong spot gold was indicated at $385.50/$386 an ounce at midday on Friday, down from both the New York market's close at $385.50/$386 an ounce on Thursday and the earlier London afternoon fix at $386.

Dealers in Singapore noted that talk of large sell-orders above the market, reported to be in Swiss hands, and concentrated around the $388 area is also weighing on the market. Active selling of short-dated call options was reported towards the $388 level.
Bullion's probe on the downside combined with the seasonal pick-up in demand has encouraged greater physical offtake in the Far East and lifted cash premums, dealers said.
Singapore gold premiums over spot London prices were quoted at between 35-55 cents an ounce compared with 25-45 cents a week ago, mainly reflecting tighter supply of Australian kilo bars.
South Korean and Indonesian-origin gold premiums were indicated steady at between 10-20 cents an ounce.

A halt to recent dishoarding by Indonesian gold holders and the sharp cutback in South Korean bullion trade, since a government crackdown on speculative arbitrage trade in July, have also allowed Singapore premiums to appreciate recently, dealers said.

Gold premiums in Hong Kong have risen gradually too, from about 10 cents an ounce about two months ago to about 30-40 cents currently, gold traders said, noting that gold imports into the British territory from South Korea had dropped.

"We've known (the South Korean crackdown) was coming for a while and it will probably allow the market to return to some sort of normalcy," said a gold trader at a large bullion firm's Hong Kong office.
South Korea's crackdown on speculative gold traders has cut by half the country's exports of the metal and put many bullion houses out of business, traders and officials said on Wednesday.
But low premiums may have helped some in Hong Kong.
"Jewellers have been buying cheap gold from South Korea and cutting their costs, South Korea has actually subsidised some and helped them survive," one source said.
Others, whose profit margins have taken a bruising, were less kind about the new measures taken by the South Korean government.
"The bottom line is that (the problem) is not going away and I for one am getting thoroughly irritated," one trader said.
He noted that South Korean chaebols (industrial conglomerates) would be likely to try and find other ways to continue arbitraging, such as switching to platinum.
Other sources countered that this was unlikely as adequate platinum supplies were hard to source for such physical trade.
With a contribution from Singapore.
--Hong Kong Newsroom (852) 2843 6358.
